rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the evidence and makes the missing proof visible instead of decorating around it. Its best move is the discipline in “Proof it needs: how ‘session’ and ‘9 minutes’ are defined,” which is exactly the question a real reporter will ask. B has sharper shop talk, but lines like “Duolingo’s 40% User Growth and Profitability Are Not a Coincidence” turn a fact pattern into a TED-stage thesis without the bridge.
gaps_in_A: “a gamified chess course” adds an adjective the update does not supply; the facts say only that a chess course launches free for all users.
“Duolingo is responding by adding more engagement-driven AI features” implies the launch is a response to educator criticism. The update gives coexistence, not motive.
“There is no current external news peg in these facts” is honest, but it leaves every angle dependent on Duolingo’s own announcement clock. That is pitchable, not durable.
gaps_in_B: “whether Duolingo is pivoting from language app to AI learning platform” is a platform-pivot claim built on one chess course and one language-practice feature. Interesting if an exec says it; invented if they do not.
“Whether It Can Replace a Human Tutor” overreaches. The update says conversation practice for paid Max users, not replacement, displacement, or pressure on tutoring platforms.

“Duolingo’s 40% User Growth and Profitability Are Not a Coincidence” asserts a causal story the supplied facts do not support. That headline needs revenue mix, conversion, retention, or management commentary.
“AI Tutoring Expensive” is not grounded. Paid Max access is in the facts; price, expense, and conversion logic are not.
